extracted.intended_audience: users and authors of Metamath databases: mathematicians, formalizers, and programmers who write/verify formal proofs with the Metamath program
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and verifying formal mathematical statements, declarations, and proofs in the Metamath language and producing/maintaining Metamath database source files and outputs (LaTeX/HTML).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath language simplicity / minimalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification of the Metamath language is only four pages long; its language is very small and intentionally simple; it treats all mathematical statements as mere sequences of symbols and has almost no hard-wired syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design databases and source files to follow the small, fixed token-based syntax. Prefer expressing everything as tokens/strings and use the Metamath tooling to map tokens to presentation (LaTeX/HTML). Simplicity reduces parser complexity and makes automatic processing easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must be machine-verified (proof verifier principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program is a proof verifier: the program verifies proofs that you supply; once a proof is verified by Metamath, it is definitely correct (assuming the verifier and axioms are correct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always run verify-proof procedures; rely on multiple independent verifiers where possible for extra confidence. Treat the Metamath verification output as the authoritative check of syntactic correctness and substitution legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath is not an automated theorem prover
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program doesn’t prove theorems automatically but is designed to verify proofs that you supply to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authoring proofs, be prepared to construct proofs manually (or use external tools that generate Metamath proofs) and use the Proof Assistant to help fill in details; do not expect the core verifier to find proofs for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal system components must be supplied
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal or mathematical system consists of symbols, syntax rules (wffs), axioms, and inference rules; you must provide these to Metamath (the language contains no mathematics per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating a database, explicitly declare tokens, syntax, axioms, and inference rules so that the Metamath verifier can operate from a well-specified foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms vs. definitions distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms and definitions should be treated differently—definitions should not be axioms unless necessary; Metamath documents an approach to definitions, including what is a definition and eliminability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer making things definitions (eliminable abbreviations) rather than adding axioms; follow the book's 'proper definition' criteria and the set.mm approach to definitions to avoid introducing unnecessary axioms or inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: $c and $v declarations for constants and variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare constants and variables explicitly using $c (constants) and $v (variables) statements in a Metamath source file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every token used as a constant or variable must be declared; follow scoping conventions and avoid redeclaring tokens incorrectly. Use the declarations before using tokens in assertions or statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: $f (type) and $e (essential) statements for variable typing and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Use $f statements to declare variable type (typecode) hypotheses and $e statements for essential (syntactic/logical) hypotheses required by assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include necessary $f and $e statements so that each assertion has its variable-type and essential hypotheses explicitly present; these are part of an assertion's preconditions and must be supplied for proofs to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: $d statements for disjoint-variable constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare disjoint-variable restrictions using $d statements to prevent variable capture and to satisfy substitution provisos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all required disjoint-variable constraints appear; the disjoint-variable restriction is mandatory where indicated and prevents improper substitutions that would make a proof invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion forms: axiomatic and provable assertions ($a and $p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use $a for axiomatic (axiom) assertions and $p for provable assertions (theorems); also be aware of forms like deduction form, inference form, and closed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the correct assertion form: axioms ($a) for base rules, $p for theorems. When formalizing, document whether an assertion is in deduction, inference, or closed form and follow the examples/spec for each form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper substitution and handling of free/bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitutions must be proper: variables must be replaced in a way that respects free and bound occurrences and avoids capture; the Metamath spec emphasizes proper substitution and distinct-variable provisos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing proofs, check free-variable occurrences, ensure substitutions obey the mandatory disjoint-variable restrictions, and follow the spec's rules for proper substitution to avoid invalid proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory declarations and hypotheses (mandatory $d, mandatory hypothesis/variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain declarations and hypotheses are mandatory (e.g., mandatory $d statements, mandatory variable-type hypotheses and mandatory hypotheses) and must appear for assertions to be well-formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that every assertion and its proof include all required mandatory declarations and hypotheses; the verifier will reject assertions lacking these mandatory components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof formats: normal, compressed, compact, Lemmon/tree styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath supports multiple proof formats: normal proofs, compressed proofs, compact proofs, Lemmon-style, and tree-style proofs; compressed proofs and a 'compact' format are documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate proof format for your goals (readability vs size). If using compressed proofs, follow the compressed-proof specification exactly (alphabet mapping, label references); for human-readable proofs prefer normal or tree-style and use the Proof Assistant to generate or verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frames and scoping statements (${ and $}) for local declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scoping statements (${ and $}) and Frames to create local scopes (local variables, local labels) and to manage nested blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encapsulate local declarations and proofs within frames to avoid polluting the global namespace; understand nested block behavior and scope nesting levels to ensure declarations are visible where needed but not elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Proof Assistant CLI commands in proof construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program provides a Proof Assistant and numerous CLI commands (prove, let, match, unify, assign, improve, save new_proof, etc.) to help build proofs interactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authoring proofs interactively, learn and use the listed commands properly (and their qualifiers/options) to construct and iteratively improve proofs. Use save and verify commands frequently to avoid losing progress and to check correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and error checking commands (verify proof / verify markup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use verify proof and verify markup commands to check proofs and markup; error checking and verify markup facilities exist to detect mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run verification commands after changes; use show trace_back, show usage, and other diagnostic commands when verification fails to locate and fix errors in proofs or source files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling conventions and label sequences (assertion labels, hypothesis labels, local labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels identify assertions and hypotheses; there are global and local label modes and label sequences are used in proofs and compressed proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent labeling for assertions and hypotheses. When writing proofs, ensure label sequences refer to the correct labels (local vs global) and use show labels / show statement to inspect label declarations and associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating vs. essential hypotheses and hypothesis association
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation between floating hypotheses (variable-type hypotheses) and essential hypotheses; hypothesis association rules determine which hypotheses accompany assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each theorem/assertion, ensure floating and essential hypotheses are declared and associated correctly; failure to provide required hypothesis associations will cause verification failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification and handling ambiguous unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath performs unification during proof construction and verification; ambiguous unification can occur and the system has unification timeouts and controls (set unification timeout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of ambiguous unification cases and use set unification timeout, set search limit, and other configuration commands. When ambiguous unification arises, restructure steps or add constraints (e.g., disjoint-variable restrictions) to remove ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed proof format rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed proofs use a compact encoding and require following the compressed-proof specification (mapping of labels to alphabet, RPN order rules, compressed proof alphabet, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate compressed proofs only after the normal proof is correct or via tools that build them. Verify compressed-proof syntax carefully (use verify proof / verify markup) and consult appendix/examples for the exact format.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPN (reverse Polish) proof stack discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath proofs are often represented using an RPN stack; RPN order and stack operations (push/pop) must be respected when writing and parsing proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building or reading proofs, track the RPN stack state precisely. Errors in push/pop order or RPN sequences lead to incorrect proofs; use show proof and RPN diagnostic commands to inspect the stack behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: File inclusion and modular organization of source files
rubrics_metrics.description: Files may include other files; use the documented include mechanisms ($[ and $], including other files) and manage file naming conventions (Unix/Mac) properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize large developments into multiple files and include them using the documented include statements. Keep path/name conventions platform-appropriate and ensure included files are readable by the Metamath program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting and presentation comments ($t) and additional info ($j)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use $t comments for typesetting (LaTeX) information and $j comments for additional information; the Metamath program can convert tokens to LaTeX and generate HTML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide $t definitions mapping tokens to LaTeX where desired for readable output. Use $j for bibliographic or explanatory notes. Generate LaTeX/HTML using the provided write commands to produce readable documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating LaTeX and HTML output
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program can output LaTeX and HTML; there are commands and comment types to control HTML/LaTeX generation (open tex/close tex, write theorem_list, write bibliography, htmldef, htmltitle, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate source with typesetting and html comments as needed, then run the appropriate write/open commands to create publication-quality outputs. Verify markup and generated output for consistency with source assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and size limitations awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath has size and memory limitations (size limitations in Metamath, show memory command); source formatting commands (set width/height/scroll) affect CLI behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor show memory and manage large databases carefully (splitting files, using compressed proofs). Adjust CLI display parameters as needed; be aware of practical limits when creating very large developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scoping statements for frames and local variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames and scoping statements control the visibility of declarations; scoping statements (${ and $}) and frame constructs are used to encapsulate variable declarations and local labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scoping to keep local variables/labels local to proofs/subproofs. Understand nesting and outermost blocks to avoid name conflicts and accidental redeclarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Metamath EBNF and syntactic specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath language syntax is specified (including an EBNF in Appendix E) and parsers rely on this restricted spec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere strictly to the syntax in the spec/EBNF when writing source files; small deviations can break parsers and verifiers. Use the documented auxiliary keywords and print-safe tokenization (ASCII) rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typecodes and variable-type hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables have typecodes and variable-type hypotheses (typecode/type) must be declared to indicate allowable syntactic roles for variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign and declare correct typecodes for variables via $f statements; ensure assertions include variable-type hypotheses so the verifier can check correct usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implicit axioms — make assumptions explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't introduce hidden or implicit axioms; all axioms and necessary assumptions should be explicitly stated so the database can be thoroughly verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing mathematics pay attention to implicit assumptions in informal proofs and encode them explicitly as axioms or derivable lemmas to prevent inconsistency or incorrect inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper, eliminable definitions (definition quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition should be 'proper' in that it can be eliminated and should not add independent content as an axiom would; creative definitions are allowed but must be examined for eliminability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining new notions, prefer definitions that can be expanded/eliminated. Follow the approach to definitions in set.mm and add constraints if necessary to ensure correctness and avoid unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof length and complexity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs can be long and tedious to construct; proof length is a practical concern and there are tools (Proof Assistant, mmj2, Holophrasm conversions) and compressed formats to manage size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance human readability and proof compactness. Use existing lemmas and the Proof Assistant to shorten proofs; when optimizing proof length, test via independent verifiers to be confident in correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent verifiers for confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple independently-implemented Metamath verifiers increase confidence in the correctness of a database; the set.mm database is verified by several verifiers in different languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where high assurance is required, verify critical databases with more than one verifier implementation. This guards against bugs in an individual verifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify and follow operator/keyword usage and whitespace/token rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath uses ASCII tokens and has rules about printable characters, tokenization, and whitespace; special characters and auxiliary keywords ($., $=, $[ $], etc.) have exact meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the spec's token/keyword usage precisely. Use the approved printable ASCII for tokens and adhere to whitespace rules so parsers and the verifier interpret source files consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hypotheses association and essential hypothesis labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis association (which optional/mandatory hypotheses apply to an assertion) must be correct; hypothesis labels and associations determine the preconditions of theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that every proof step refers to labels whose hypotheses are compatible; use show statement and show labels to inspect associations when debugging verification failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction theorem forms and deduction style (Standard/Weak Deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath documents the standard deduction theorem, the weak deduction theorem, deduction style, and natural deduction forms; certain forms of assertions reflect these styles (deduction form, inference form, closed form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encoding proofs that use deduction-style transformations, choose the correct form and follow the book's guidance about rearranging hypotheses and the implications for variable scoping and substitution.
